newsitem.title: USA: Odd couple Albright-Helms meet in senator's state.
newsitem.headline: Odd couple Albright-Helms meet in senator's state.

text.p: The university student earnestly asked U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright on Tuesday what she considered her toughest diplomatic negotiation.
"Jesse Helms," Albright shot back with a devillish grin on her face.

The audience erupted in laughter and so did the man in question, influential Republican Sen. Jesse Helms, who was seated at a creaky school desk in the front row of the Wingate University classroom where Albright was holding court.

The secretary of state quickly corrected herself, saying her biggest negotiating thorn really was China, when as U.N. ambassador she tried to persude Beijing to back an extended peacekeeping mission in Haiti.

But there was at least a half-truth to her original answer and that was why the Clinton administration's media celebrity spent a second full day in a year in Helms' home state of North Carolina, talking about foreign policy to community leaders, businessmen and students.

Helms is Republican chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee who has been blocking key U.S. foreign initiatives, including ratification of the Chemical Weapons Convention and incresed foreign affairs funding.
Albright has spent countless hours trying to woo the stubborn 75-year-old senator into a more cooperative bipartisan foreign policy and it seems to be working.
She started out her day in North Carolina telling community leaders she came to the state with "realistic expectations."
When she visited Helms on his home turf last year, her efforts to persuade him of the correctness of administration foreign policy positions "didn't change his view one bit."
But on Tuesday, Albright had better results.

While some may debate her personal role, Helms used a news conference with the secretary to publicly signal his willigness to negotiate on the chemical arms pact -- a Clinton-Albright priority -- and to predict Senate ratification was possible.
In many ways, they are a Washington odd-couple -- Albright, the administration's most articulate foreign policy spokesman, and Helms, the administration's crusty arch-conservative foe.
But there is unquestionably affection and respect between them, which was on display as Helms escorted Albright from event to event.
"I would say the chemistry is very good," Albright told reporters.
"We agree on the large issues, that being the importance of protecting American national interests, and when we disagree we're pretty straight about it. We can talk about our differences," she said.
"We are developing a pretty solid friendship," she added.
Helms, known for his courtly ways, was more than gracious. "You bet. She's a favourite of my family already," he said, before entertaining Albright at a private dinner with his family.
They walked out of the meeting with the students arm in arm and Albright planned to give the senator a navy-blue T-shirt that reads: "Somebody in the State Department loves me."
Albright won credibility with Helms by forcing the ouster of U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali to make way for a U.N. chief viewed as more willing to make reforms.

As an immigrant from Czechoslovakia who came to the United States after the Second World War, she also has connected with him on their deep feeling for democratic values and for opposition to Fidel Castro's communist Cuba.
Now she is trying to convince him to support a plan to pay more than $1 billion in back dues to the United Nations and to increase spending for other foreign affairs accounts.
"Senator Helms and I agree on the need for a strong American foreign policy. But when it comes to paying for that policy, we do not always agree on the 'how much' or the 'what for,'" Albright said.
